beats.caption: In 1958 the US Air Force paid for a study on setting off a nuclear bomb on the Moon. Meatball opened the file. #coldwar #weirdhistory #meatballinvestigates
sources: Wikipedia, Project A119: top-secret 1958 US Air Force plan, run at the Armour Research Foundation (Chicago) and led by Leonard Reiffel, to detonate a nuclear bomb on the Moon, partly as a show of strength during the space race after Sputnik; Carl Sagan modelled the expansion of the dust cloud; abandoned in January 1959 — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Project_A119 (FACTDESK: verify)
Leonard Reiffel, 'A Study of Lunar Research Flights', Vol. I, Armour Research Foundation, 19 June 1959 (AFSWC-TR-59-39, DTIC AD0425380), declassified — FACTDESK: verify the report number
The Observer/Guardian, May 2000: Reiffel confirms the US planned to explode a nuclear bomb on the Moon so the flash would be visible from Earth — FACTDESK: find and cite the exact article

Keay Davidson, 'Carl Sagan: A Life' (1999): Sagan referenced the classified project in a 1959 application for a Miller Institute graduate fellowship at UC Berkeley — FACTDESK: verify wording ('fellowship application', not 'job application')

beats.say: The US Air Force paid for it. But why?

beats.say: Subscribe. I investigate weird stuff daily.
See, in 1958, the Soviets had just launched Sputnik.
America was losing the space race, and everybody could see it.
So why bomb the Moon? Guess.
Guess one: blast a hole for a moon base. Nope. Nobody was going up yet.
Guess two: aliens. I checked. No aliens in the file. Phew.
Wait. The plan says the flash had to be visible from Earth.
It was a warning. A flash on the Moon the whole world could watch.
It was called Project A119. The report is real, and it's public now.
One young scientist worked out how the dust cloud would spread. Carl Sagan.

shots.photo: Carl Sagan, NASA public domain photo only

beats.say: They dropped it in 1959. Too risky, and people would have hated it.
The Moon is round. I'm round. I'm taking this personally.
And the world only found out because Sagan mentioned the secret project on a fellowship application.
Would you have pushed the button? Comment.
